lesson.title: Anatomy of an Ethernet Frame: How Bits Become Messages
lesson.summary: The Ethernet frame is the envelope that carries every packet across a local network, wrapping data in header and trailer fields that identify sender, receiver, and payload type. Understanding its structure explains why frames have size limits and how switches read just enough of a frame to forward it correctly.
lesson.body:
Every time a computer on a local network needs to send data, it doesn't just fling raw bits onto the wire. It wraps the data in an Ethernet frame, a structured envelope defined by the IEEE 802.3 Ethernet standard. If a network-layer packet, say an IP packet, is the letter being mailed, the Ethernet frame is the physical envelope: it adds a destination address, a return address, and a few other fields the local network hardware needs to route and verify delivery. This is the general pattern for any frame at the link layer, but Ethernet's specific field layout is what every switch, network card, and packet analyzer on a LAN actually reads.

A standard Ethernet II frame has a well defined layout. It opens with a 7 byte preamble and a 1 byte start of frame delimiter, a repeating bit pattern that lets the receiving network interface card synchronize its clock before real data arrives. Next come two 6 byte MAC addresses: the destination address first, then the source address, each a globally unique hardware identifier assigned to the network card. After the addresses sits a 2 byte EtherType field, which tells the receiving device what kind of payload follows, such as 0x0800 for IPv4, 0x0806 for ARP, or 0x86DD for IPv6. The payload itself, the actual packet being carried, follows and can range from 46 to 1500 bytes. The frame closes with a 4 byte Frame Check Sequence, a CRC checksum the sender computes over the frame so the receiver can detect transmission errors.

Those size boundaries are not arbitrary. The 1500 byte maximum payload, known as the standard Ethernet MTU, still shapes internet performance today, since a packet larger than the smallest MTU along its path must be fragmented or dropped. The 64 byte minimum frame size has a more subtle history: on early shared media Ethernet, a sending station needed to still be transmitting when notice of a collision could reach it from the far end of the cable, so frames were padded with zeros if the real payload was too short to meet that minimum. Even now that most Ethernet runs on switched, collision free links, the 64 byte floor remains part of the standard for compatibility.

Consider a laptop printing a document to a network printer sitting on the same office LAN. The laptop's operating system hands an IP packet down to the network card, which already knows the printer's MAC address from a previous lookup. The card builds a frame: destination MAC set to the printer's hardware address, source MAC set to the laptop's own address, EtherType set to 0x0800 to mark an IPv4 payload, the IP packet inserted as the frame's data, and a freshly computed FCS appended at the end. That frame, now somewhere between 64 and 1518 bytes depending on the document data, goes out on the wire. Any switch between the laptop and the printer reads only the destination MAC address to decide where to forward it; it does not need to open the IP packet at all.

The FCS matters because Ethernet itself makes no promises about delivery. When a receiving network card recomputes the CRC over an incoming frame and it does not match the FCS, the card simply discards the frame, with no automatic retransmission at the link layer. If reliable delivery matters, that job falls to a higher layer, typically TCP, which notices the missing data through a timeout or missing acknowledgment and requests it again. This split, Ethernet handling local delivery and error detection while upper layers handle reliability, is a recurring theme in networking and one reason the frame format stays lean rather than solving every problem on its own.
